speaker: Terence Tao
title: Terence Tao: Hardest Problems in Mathematics, Physics & the Future of AI (#472)
question: In scientific and mathematical discovery, why does training AI on published research literature fall short of enabling models to generate novel laws or conjectures?
guest: Current models struggle a lot with this. Physicists have a dream of feeding AI all this data so it says, 'Here's a new pattern we didn't see before.' But the state of the art even struggles to rediscover old laws of physics from data—and when it does, there's a big concern with contamination, that it only succeeded because somewhere in its training data it already knew Boyle's law or whatever law you're trying to reconstruct. Part of it is we don't have the right type of training data. For laws of physics, we don't have a million different universes with a million different laws of nature. And in math, what we're missing is the negative space: we have published papers of things people proved and conjectures that were verified, but we don't have data on conjectures that were good things to try, turned out wrong, and then got modified to become more plausible. That trial-and-error process is an integral part of human mathematical discovery, which we don't record because it's embarrassing—we only like to publish our wins. So AI has no access to that data to train on.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Published literature records the polished end products of discovery, not the process that produced them. Papers present final theorems, laws, and clean proofs, while omitting the failed attempts, dead ends, abandoned conjectures, intuitions, heuristics, and iterative back-and-forth between hypothesis and evidence that actually led there. A model trained on this corpus learns to reproduce and recombine the finished artifacts, and to write in the style of results, but gets little signal about how to search an open problem space, judge which questions are worth asking, or recognise when an idea is promising.

Several related gaps compound this. The literature is biased toward positive results, so models rarely see what doesn't work. Training objectives reward predicting plausible, consensus text, which pulls toward interpolation within known ideas rather than extrapolation beyond them. And discovery requires a feedback loop with reality, such as running experiments, testing conjectures against data or counterexamples, and revising, which static text cannot supply.

This is why researchers argue progress needs process-level data and closed-loop systems that generate, test, and refine hypotheses, rather than more papers alone.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Published research records the sanitized endpoints of discovery rather than the generative process behind it. Papers present polished, post-hoc justifications of successful results while omitting the messy exploration where breakthroughs actually take shape: raw intuitions, failed experiments, dead-end proofs, and informative counterexamples. Because of this publication bias, models trained solely on literature learn to imitate the form of settled knowledge without learning how to navigate uncertainty, diagnose failure, or revise flawed assumptions.

Furthermore, statistical learning over text favors interpolation within existing paradigms. While models excel at recombining known concepts, genuinely novel laws and conjectures often require inventing new abstractions or overturning consensus assumptions outside the training distribution. Finally, static text provides no causal or logical feedback loop with an external source of truth. Without active experimentation, simulation, or formal verification, a model cannot generate new data, confront empirical anomalies, falsify bold hypotheses, or distinguish genuine insight from plausible-sounding confabulation.

Papers present polished, retroactive justifications and confirmed results while omitting the dead ends, failed conjectures, intuition-building examples, and iterative refinements where genuine insight actually forms. Training solely on this curated archive introduces severe survivorship bias: a model observes what turned out to be true, not how researchers navigate uncertainty, spot anomalies, or recognize when an established framework breaks down. Furthermore, predicting tokens over existing text rewards statistical interpolation within prevailing paradigms, whereas formulating a novel law or conjecture demands abductive, out-of-distribution leaps that often overturn consensus assumptions. Finally, static text provides no interactive grounding or falsification. Scientific and mathematical breakthroughs rely on an active feedback loop—proposing hypotheses, probing edge cases against physical experiments or formal proof verifiers, and revising directly from failure. Without access to full search trajectories and closed-loop verification, models become fluent synthesizers of known results rather than originators of new theory.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Published papers record the results of discovery, not how the discovery happened. A paper presents a polished, logically ordered argument that usually runs in the opposite order from how the idea arose. It leaves out the failed attempts, the abandoned conjectures, the heuristic guesses, the numerical experiments, and the tacit judgment about what seemed promising, which are the parts that actually lead to new laws. Publication bias makes this worse, because negative results and dead ends rarely appear in print. A model trained on this corpus therefore learns what successful conclusions look like, but not how to search for them.

These models are also mainly trained to reproduce the statistical patterns of existing text. That lets them interpolate and recombine known ideas fluently, but a genuinely new law or conjecture lies outside that distribution and often contradicts the consensus of the time. Discovery also depends on contact with reality: raw data, experiments, computation, and checking ideas against them, so that wrong guesses get rejected. This is why the more successful systems, such as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve, pair a language model with external evaluators and a loop of exploring, testing and refining, rather than relying on the literature alone.

Published papers mostly record the end of discovery. They present laws that survived testing and proofs that were worked out, while often leaving out failed guesses, overlooked patterns, and the choices that led researchers to the right experiment or example. Training on papers can teach a model the concepts and forms of scientific reasoning, but it gives the model fewer opportunities to practice deciding what to try next and learning from the result.

An AI can still propose novel laws or conjectures from what it learns in the literature. The harder part is telling which ideas are worth pursuing. Several laws can fit the same observations, and a conjecture can hold in every example tried and still be false. Distinguishing promising ideas from plausible-sounding ones requires feedback from new observations, experiments, computations, or attempts to find proofs and counterexamples.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Published papers usually show the finished argument. A physicist may report a law that fits the data without describing the rival explanations that failed or the observation that suggested a useful variable. A mathematician may publish a conjecture and its proof while leaving out the examples and counterexamples that shaped the original guess. The literature therefore gives a model many examples of what successful discoveries look like and fewer examples of how to make one.

Training on that record can help a model propose something new. But a claim can sound like published science or mathematics and still be false, trivial, or already known. Evaluating a proposed law requires testing its predictions against observations, ideally where rival laws predict different outcomes. Evaluating a conjecture involves checking prior work, looking for counterexamples, and ultimately seeking a proof. Learning from papers helps generate candidates, but on its own it supplies only part of that feedback.
